lesson.title: Dot products and length

lead.text: Take a smaller field to check the idea, one that is 8 m across and 15 m up. The two sides you would walk meet at a right angle, and the straight line between the corners is the long side of the triangle they make. Pythagoras's rule says that the square on the long side equals the sum of the squares on the two short sides.

Squaring the sides gives 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289, so the shortcut is the square root of 289, which is 17 m. The same recipe finds the length of any vector (x, y). Square each coordinate and add the two squares. The square root of that total is the length of the vector, and it is never negative.

afterFigure.text: The picture draws a square on each side of the right-angled triangle. Turning the field round, from (8, 15) to (15, 8), gives a different vector with the same length, because the same two squares are added.

lead.text: The walk from one corner of the field to the opposite corner is a vector: 9 across and 12 up.

reveal.text: You squared 9 and 12 and added the squares, then took the square root. That recipe gives the length of any vector.

lead.text: The sum of squares follows a pattern. Each coordinate is multiplied by itself and the two results are added. The same pattern works on two different vectors. Take (2, 5) and (1, 3). Multiply the across numbers together and the up numbers together. Then add the two products: 2 × 1 + 5 × 3 = 17.
This is called the dot product. We write it with a dot between the vectors, so (2, 5) · (1, 3) = 17. The answer is one number, a scalar with no across and up parts.

Now put the same vector on both sides of the dot. The dot product of (8, 15) with itself is 8 × 8 + 15 × 15 = 289, exactly the number you added up to find the length. A vector's dot product with itself is its length squared, so its length is the square root of that dot product.
Multiply matching coordinates and add the products. The answer is a single number.

reveal.text: You multiplied 1 × 3 and 2 × 4, then added 3 and 8. A dot product always ends as one number.

lead.text: Coordinates can be negative, so it is worth checking what a minus sign does. A length squares each coordinate first, and a negative number times itself is positive: (−8)² = 64, the same as 8². The vectors (8, 15) and (−8, 15) end up with the same length, 17. Length ignores direction.

In a dot product the signs matter more. A positive number times a negative one gives a negative product, and the two products can pull against each other. For (3, 1) · (−2, 5) the products are −6 and 5, which add to −1. A dot product can come out negative. A vector dotted with itself cannot, since each of its products is a number times itself.

workedSteps.text: Square each coordinate and add. This is the vector's dot product with itself.
The length is the positive square root.
Add the two products. What is the dot product?

lead.text: Dot a vector with itself and every product is a number times itself. Keep the signs as you go.

reveal.text: Each product was a number times itself, so both came out positive. A vector's dot product with itself is never negative.

lead.text: A vector built from a journey has a second reading. The pair (across, up) says which way a traveller went from her start. Its length says how far from the start she ended up in a straight line, whatever route she took. With coordinates in kilometres, the length comes out in kilometres too, since the square root undoes the squaring and returns the unit.

A hiker whose displacement is (−8, −15) kilometres has gone 8 km west and 15 km south. Her distance from the start is √(64 + 225) = 17 km. The path she took may have been longer. The vector only records where she ended up, so its length is the distance a bird would fly.

diagram.caption: The vector (−8, −15) records only where the hiker ended up. Its length, 17 km, is the straight-line distance, whatever path she walked.

blocks.text: A rectangular field is 9 m wide and 12 m long. You stand at one corner and want to reach the opposite one. You can walk along two sides, which is 9 m and then 12 m, so 21 m in all. A gap in the hedge lets you cut straight across, and the straight line is clearly shorter.

How much shorter depends on a rule you may remember from school, and the rule belongs to vectors. The walk to the far corner is the vector (9, 12), which is 9 across and 12 up. Its length is the distance of the straight route.
This lesson finds the length of a vector from its coordinates. Along the way we meet a new way of combining two vectors that gives a single number and has a length hidden inside it.

diagram.alt: A rectangular field drawn to scale, 9 m wide and 12 m long. One route follows two sides from the bottom left corner to the top right corner. A second route cuts straight across the diagonal and is plainly shorter.
diagram.caption: Two ways to the opposite corner. Walking round the edge is 21 m. The straight line across is shorter.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a vector's length from its coordinates and calculate the dot product of two vectors.

recap.keyIdea: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products into one number. A vector's dot product with itself is its squared length.

blocks.text: Back at the field, you can now say how long the shortcut is from its sides alone. You found that (2, 1) · (3, −2) = 4, that (−7, 24) is 25 long, and that a minus sign cannot change a length because squaring removes it.

recap.nextHook: You can now measure any vector. The next lesson shrinks a 10 m step to exactly 1 m in the same direction, and finds out what it means when a dot product comes to zero.
